content: Metronidazole is indicated for the treatment of symptomatic trichomoniasis caused by Trichomonas vaginalis in both females and males. The diagnosis must be confirmed through appropriate laboratory methods, such as wet smears or cultures. Metronidazole is also indicated for the treatment of asymptomatic trichomoniasis in females when the organism is associated with conditions such as endocervicitis, cervicitis, or cervical erosion. Since the presence of Trichomonas vaginalis can interfere with the accurate interpretation of abnormal cytological smears, additional smears should be performed after the parasite has been eradicated. For the treatment of asymptomatic sexual partners, it is important to note that Trichomonas vaginalis is a sexually transmitted infection. Asymptomatic sexual partners of treated patients should be treated simultaneously if the organism is detected, to prevent reinfection. The decision to treat an asymptomatic male partner who has a negative culture or has not undergone culture testing should be individualized. Evidence suggests that reinfection in women can occur if their sexual partner is not treated. Additionally, isolating the organism from asymptomatic male carriers can be challenging, and negative smears or cultures cannot be solely relied upon. In cases of reinfection, the sexual partner should be treated with metronidazole. Metronidazole is indicated for the treatment of acute intestinal amebiasis (amebic dysentery) and amebic liver abscess. In cases of amebic liver abscess, metronidazole therapy does not eliminate the need for aspiration or drainage of pus. Metronidazole is also indicated for the treatment of serious infections caused by susceptible anaerobic bacteria. Surgical procedures, when indicated, should be performed in conjunction with metronidazole therapy. In mixed infections involving both aerobic and anaerobic bacteria, additional antimicrobials appropriate for the aerobic infection should be used alongside metronidazole. Specific indications for anaerobic bacterial infections include: Intra-abdominal infections, such as peritonitis, intra-abdominal abscess, and liver abscess, caused by Bacteroides species (including the Bacteroides fragilis group: B. fragilis, B. distasonis, B. ovatus, B. thetaiotaomicron, B. vulgatus), Clostridium species, Eubacterium species, Peptococcus species, or Peptostreptococcus species. Skin and skin structure infections caused by Bacteroides species (including the B. fragilis group), Clostridium species, Peptococcus species, Peptostreptococcus species, or Fusobacterium species. Gynecologic infections, including endometritis, endomyometritis, tubo-ovarian abscess, and post-surgical vaginal cuff infections, caused by Bacteroides species (including the B. fragilis group), Clostridium species, Peptococcus species, Peptostreptococcus species, or Fusobacterium species. Bacterial septicemia caused by Bacteroides species (including the B. fragilis group) or Clostridium species. Bone and joint infections (as adjunctive therapy) caused by Bacteroides species (including the B. fragilis group). Central nervous system infections, including meningitis and brain abscess, caused by Bacteroides species (including the B. fragilis group). Lower respiratory tract infections, including pneumonia, empyema, and lung abscess, caused by Bacteroides species (including the B. fragilis group). Endocarditis caused by Bacteroides species (including the B. fragilis group). To minimize the development of drug-resistant bacteria and maintain the effectiveness of metronidazole and other antibacterial drugs, metronidazole should only be used to treat or prevent infections that are proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. When culture and susceptibility data are available, they should guide the selection or modification of antibacterial therapy. In the absence of such data, local epidemiology and susceptibility patterns may inform empiric therapy decisions.
